newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: BIS offers membership to nine central banks.
newsitem.headline: BIS offers membership to nine central banks.

text.p: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS), central bank to the world's central banks, said its board of directors would invite nine central banks to become members of the BIS by subscribing to BIS shares.

Wim Duisenberg, BIS chairman and chairman of the Dutch central bank, told a news conference the invited central banks were Hong Kong Monetary Authority, The People's Bank of China, Banco Central do Brasil, Reserve Bank of India, Bank of Korea, Banco de Mexico, Central Bank of the Russian Federation, Saudia Arabian Monetary Agency and the Monetary Authority of Singapore.
"It is a goal to let the BIS play a more global role over time than has been the case in the past," Duisenberg told reporters.
Duisenberg said the decision to invite the nine banks was made at a meeting of the BIS board.
The new members will not change the decision-making structure of the BIS, which is headed by a board of directors made up of the Group of 10 (G10) industrial nations.
Total membership of the BIS is now 32 central banks, all of which are either European or North American with the exception of Japan, Australia and South Africa.

As members, the nine new central banks will be able to participate in cooperative activities of the BIS and have an influence on common views, which often emerge as the basis for recommendations in areas such as financial regulation and payment systems, Duisenberg said.
Duisenberg said the election of the nine new members was based on representative economic and financial criteria and on their involvement in world economic and financial cooperation.
"Seven of the nine countries...are the largest economies in their respective regions, while Hong Kong and Singapore both have major financial markets," he said.
He said the admission process would be finished by March 1997 at the latest.
To become members, the nine central banks will have to buy shares in the BIS.

Duisenberg said the BIS would not disclose how many shares were involved in the transaction but said there would be no need to increase the BIS authorised share capital of 1.5 billion gold francs (1 gold franc = $1.94). -- Zurich Editorial +41 1 631 7340
